---
title: "Where you are now"
---

Open your course repository and run `git log --oneline`. The newest commit is at
the top, so scroll down to the very first one, the one from September, and read
your way back up. A to-do list turns into a class blog. A bracelet editor grows
a test file. Somewhere near the top a browser starts clicking through your app
without you, and the last commits belong to a project nobody specified for you.
This short chapter is the pause between that log and whatever you build next.

## What you carry out of this book {#sec-closing-what-you-have}

Read the part titles in the table of contents from the top. Every part added one
idea, and each idea only worked because the part before it was already yours.

- **A page is a tree of objects.** You find elements with a selector, change
  them, build new ones, and hand them event listeners. The DOM is the browser's
  living model of the page, not the file on your disk, which is why your code
  can change it while it runs (@sec-elements-are-objects-dom).
- **Pictures you can address.** An SVG shape is an element like any other, so
  the code that changes a heading also moves a circle. You scaled real numbers
  into a chart that fits its box (@sec-charts-scale) and asked the browser for
  one frame at a time (@sec-animation-loop).
- **Classes of your own.** Fields, a constructor, methods, `private` for what
  nobody outside should touch, `extends` for what two classes share, and an
  abstract member every subclass fills in differently. A variable typed as the
  base class calls that member without asking which kind it holds
  (@sec-polymorphism-name).
- **Errors that travel.** `throw` stops the code where the problem is, and the
  `catch` far above decides what the user reads on the page
  (@sec-exceptions-where).
- **Proof instead of hope.** Tests that read like sentences, arranged the same
  way every time (@sec-vitest-aaa), `npm run verify` before a commit, and a
  workflow that runs the same checks on a computer that is not yours
  (@sec-verify-ci-workflow).
- **One class, any type.** A type parameter is a hole in a class that the caller
  fills, which is how `Stack<number>` and `Stack<Command>` come from one file
  (@sec-generics-type-parameter).
- **Structures made of boxes and pointers.** A linked list, a stack, a queue,
  each built from your own `Node<T>` with no array hiding inside. You can also
  say why a queue and not a stack, in two questions
  (@sec-choosing-questions).
- **A project other people can trust.** Playwright drives the real app in a real
  browser using the words a user sees (@sec-playwright-locators), and your
  `AGENTS.md` tells the next agent, or the next human, how this project works
  (@sec-skills-agents-md).

None of that is a school version of the real thing. `class`, `extends`,
`private`, `Map`, `describe`, and `page.getByRole` are the words somebody types
at work on a Monday morning. Your apps were small so that every part of them
stayed visible on one screen, and that is the whole difference.

## Habits worth more than any keyword {#sec-closing-habits}

Keywords are easy to look up again. Three things from this year are harder to
find in a reference, and they are the ones to keep.

**Design before you type.** You drew the aquarium as boxes and arrows before a
single class existed (@sec-class-diagrams-mermaid), and you wrote the bracelet's
model before its page (@sec-bracelet-model). Ten minutes with a pen costs less
than an afternoon spent rewriting a class that carries the wrong fields.

**Red before green.** Every structure in Part 7 started with a test that failed
because the method did not exist yet (@sec-undo-experiment). A test written
afterwards only proves that the code does what the code does. A test written
first says what the code should do, and the red run tells you the test itself
works before you trust it.

**Explain every line, especially now.** You had a coding buddy all year, and the
Part 8 one writes a whole class while you watch. That makes the rule from
your first week heavier rather than lighter (@sec-buddy-what). The exam happens
without internet and without AI (@sec-from-canvas-to-page-rules), so the honest
test is whether you can rebuild something from this book and your own notes.
Outside the exam the reason is different and it does not go away: the line you
cannot explain is the line that breaks on the day somebody is watching, and no
agent will stand next to you and take the blame for it.

## Keep the repository alive {#sec-closing-keep-going}

The folder on your computer does not disappear when the course ends, and neither
does what you know. Until your next programming lessons start, build something
small. Give the beehive a second bee and a rule about who moves first. Put a
waiting time on the salon screen. Let Paint remember the drawing after a reload.
Redraw the energy chart with numbers you actually care about, your bus times or
your phone battery over a week. Take the bracelet editor and make it something
you would show a friend.

None of it has to be good. What matters is that you open VS Code with nobody
asking you to, and that the session still ends the way it did all year, with
`npm run verify`, a commit, and a push (@sec-git-loop).

## TypeScript worth researching on your own {#sec-closing-typescript}

This book taught the TypeScript the course needed and stopped there. You are now
at the point where you can read about a feature in the morning and use it the
same afternoon, which is exactly what the research boxes were training. The
[TypeScript handbook](https://www.typescriptlang.org/docs/handbook/intro.html)
is the reference for the language itself, and MDN stays the reference for
everything the browser does.

### Types that describe your data more exactly {#sec-closing-types}

- **`interface`, and how it differs from a class.** An interface describes the
  shape an object must have and carries no code at all. Look up why a class can
  promise to match an interface, and when people reach for `interface` instead
  of `type`.
- **Discriminated unions and narrowing.** You already gave a variable exactly
  two allowed values (@sec-callbacks-maps-enum). Objects can carry such a tag
  too, and inside an `if` that checks the tag, the compiler knows which fields
  exist. Search the handbook for "Narrowing".
- **Utility types.** `Partial`, `Pick`, and `Record` build a new type out of one
  you already have, instead of you copying it and editing the copy.
- **`readonly` and `as const`.** Two ways to tell the compiler that data must not
  be changed after it is created, which catches a whole family of bugs before
  the program runs.

### The browser, past what this book used {#sec-closing-browser}

- **Promises, `async`, `await`, and `fetch`.** You typed `await` in every
  Playwright test and were told to keep it out of `src/`. Find out what a
  Promise is, then read MDN on the Fetch API. Asking a server for data is the
  step that turns your apps into apps that talk to the world, and everything in
  Part 8 that felt like magic gets explained on the way.
- **`localStorage` and JSON.** Your apps forget everything on reload.
  `JSON.stringify` turns an object into text, and `localStorage` keeps that text
  between visits. This one is an afternoon of work and it changes how finished
  your projects feel.
- **Custom elements.** You can define your own tag, `<my-chart>`, backed by a
  class you write. It is the DOM and your classes meeting in one place, and it is
  how a chart becomes something you reuse instead of copying it.
- **The `<canvas>` element.** Last year's p5.js was drawing on one the whole
  time. Compare it with SVG and you will understand why this book chose SVG for
  charts and would not choose it for a particle storm.
- **Accessibility.** Roles and labels are already in your vocabulary, because
  Playwright finds elements by them (@sec-playwright-locators). The same
  attributes are what a screen reader announces to somebody who never sees your
  layout.

### The craft around the code {#sec-closing-craft}

- **Complexity.** `O(1)` and `O(n)` showed up once, when an array made you shift
  every element (@sec-linked-list-costs). The notation has a whole field behind
  it, and it is how programmers compare two solutions without running either.
- **Recursion, and trees.** A method that calls itself sounds like a trick until
  you meet a structure that is shaped like a tree. The DOM is one. Your file
  system is one.
- **More design patterns.** Undo used the command pattern (@sec-undo-command).
  Observer, factory, and strategy are the next three you will recognize in code
  you did not write.
- **A framework, later.** React, Angular, Svelte, and Vue all do by machine what
  you did by hand this year, turning data into elements and keeping them in sync.
  Having done it by hand is the reason they will make sense to you.

One tool belongs here too, and it is not a topic. Learn the debugger, in VS Code
and in your browser's developer tools. A breakpoint that pauses the program and
lets you read every variable beats a fifth `console.log`, and it takes about
twenty minutes to learn.

## What comes next at school {#sec-closing-next-years}

There is no third Creative Coding book. What follows is the rest of your school's
programming lessons, and which subjects you get depends on your school and your
branch, so read this as the shape of it rather than a timetable. Databases and
the language used to query them. Programming on the server, where your code
answers requests instead of clicks. Networks, so `fetch` stops being a mystery.
More software design, in bigger teams and on longer projects, ending in a
diploma project that lasts a school year. Somewhere in there another language
arrives, usually Java, C#, or Python.

That last one worries people more than it should. A class is a class in all
three of them, `private` still hides a field, and a unit test is still arrange,
act, assert. What changes is mostly spelling. The year you spent learning what
an object is transfers whole, and so does git, and so does the habit of running
the tests before you say you are done.

Somebody who has never met you can clone your repository, run `npm install` and
`npm start`, and use what you built, with a green check mark on GitHub telling
them it works before they even click. That was not true of you twelve months
ago. Take the summer, and then push a commit that nobody assigned you.
